extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications on claim construction and the 35 U.S.C. §112 written description requirement, including how to assess whether the specification shows possession of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction as a whole (broadest reasonable interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Each Claim, Determine What the Claim as a Whole Covers. Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the entire claim including preamble language and the transitional phrase. The examiner should evaluate each claim to determine if sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble. Limitations may not be imported into the claims from the specification. Case citations: In re Morris; Bell Communications Research v. Vitalink; Corning Glass Works v. Sumitomo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble and transitional phrase treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire claim, including preamble and the transitional phrase (e.g., 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of'), must be considered in claim construction and support analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Comprising' is open-ended and allows unrecited elements; 'consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground and, absent clear specification, may be construed equivalent to 'comprising' for 102/103 purposes. If applicant contends exclusion by 'consisting essentially of', applicant bears burden to show additional steps/components would materially change characteristics. See Genentech v. Chiron; PPG Industries v. Guardian Industries; In re De Lajarte.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review entire application for support
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the claims and the entire specification, including specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings, to understand how applicant provides support for the various features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also review original claims, abstract, drawings when assessing means-plus-function support. Determine field of invention and level of skill in the art; consider inverse correlation between level of skill and specificity required. Well-known information need not be described in detail. See Wang Labs. v. Toshiba; Hybritech v. Monoclonal Antibodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description standard: possession of claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether there is sufficient written description to inform a skilled artisan that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice, clear depiction in drawings, structural chemical formulas, or any description of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics so a skilled person would recognize possession. The inquiry is factual and case-by-case. See Purdue Pharma v. Faulding; Pfaff v. Wells Electronics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence types that can show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be evidenced by reduction to practice, detailed drawings, structural/chemical formulas, sequence data, deposits, or identifying characteristics (sequence, structure, binding affinity, molecular weight, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: description of constructing an embodiment or performing a process that meets claim limitations; deposit of biological material per 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; restriction maps, mRNA isolation and expression. Drawings alone can provide written description in appropriate cases. See Cooper v. Goldfarb; Vas‑Cath; UMC Elecs.; Enzo Biochem; Noelle v. Lederman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-only definitions are generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition by function alone does not suffice to describe certain claimed subject matter (e.g., coding sequences, chemical compounds) because it indicates what the gene/compound does rather than what it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function combined with known correlation to structure may suffice in some arts; absent such correlation, function-only disclosure is little more than a wish. See Eli Lilly; Fiers; In re Wilder; Fonar (software exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical and small-molecule inventions require precise definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate written description of a chemical invention requires a precise definition by structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties, not merely a plan to obtain the chemical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification only discloses assays or methods for identifying compounds without disclosing which compounds achieve the claimed effect, the written description requirement may not be met. See Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle; examples in Fonar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6) support requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6 (means- or step-plus-function), it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must consider the original disclosure in summary, detailed description, claims, abstract, and drawings. Means-plus-function is adequately described if (1) the written description links particular structure/materials/acts to the function, or (2) one skilled in the art would know what structure/materials/acts perform the function. Rejection under 112, para. 2 cannot stand where 112, para. 1 support exists for means-plus-function recitations. See In re Noll; Supplemental Examination Guidelines; MPEP §2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis approach for claims to a single species or embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim drawn to a single embodiment or species: (A) determine whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, determine whether there is a reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed; (C) if not, determine whether the invention is set forth in distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a complete structure is disclosed, the written description requirement is satisfied for that species and a 112, para. 1 rejection must not be made. If complete structure is not disclosed, evaluate whether other identifying characteristics (partial structure, properties, function with known correlation, method of making) would lead skilled artisan to conclude applicant was in possession. See Fields v. Conover; Eli Lilly; In re Wilder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider when assessing possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider multiple factors: level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (with known correlation to structure), method of making the claimed invention, and any combination of identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The determination is factual and depends on art maturity and predictability; disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that would lead one of skill in the art to conclude possession is sufficient. See Eli Lilly; Capon v. Eshhar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of art maturity and predictability on disclosure required
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with the scientific/technologic knowledge already in existence; mature, predictable arts require less detailed disclosure than emerging, unpredictable fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mature technologies where knowledge/skill is high, a written description question generally should not be raised for claims present when originally filed, even if specification discloses only method and function (e.g., microprocessor programming). In contrast, for unpredictable or emerging technologies, more evidence is required; product-by-process claims are satisfied when the process has actually been used to produce the product, but mere description of a process without clear performability may be insufficient. See In re Hayes Microcomputer; Fiers; Amgen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base 112, para.1 rejection on absence of detail for well-established terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of definitions or details for well-established terms or procedures should not be the basis of a 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1 rejection for lack of adequate written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is conventional or well known to one of ordinary skill need not be disclosed in detail. See Hybritech v. Monoclonal Antibodies.
